mcqs.question: Why do real recommendation systems typically merge candidates from several sources (two-tower collaborative, content-based, popularity) rather than relying on one candidate-generation method?
options: Because each source covers a different gap — collaborative signal is strong for established items and users, content-based covers thin-data new items, and popularity covers cold-start users — and no single source covers all three well
Because a single candidate source is always too slow to run at request time
Because regulations require at least three independent recommendation sources
Because merging sources eliminates the need for a separate ranking stage afterward
mcqs.explanation: Merging sources is about coverage, not speed — each method has a structural blind spot (new items, new users, or reliance on volume) that a different source fills. There's no such regulatory requirement, and merged candidates still need a ranking stage to determine final order.

mcqs.question: Why is launching a new recommender without a holdout/guardrail group risky, even if it performed well offline?
options: Because holdout groups are only necessary for fraud detection systems, not recommenders
Because without a holdout there's no way to compare against what would have happened under the old system, so a slow regression on a guardrail metric can go completely undetected
Because a holdout group is required to compute offline NDCG
Because launching without a holdout makes the model impossible to roll back later
mcqs.explanation: The risk is purely about detectability — a holdout is the only way to know what the counterfactual would have been, so a regression with no holdout can go unnoticed until it's already caused damage. Holdouts aren't specific to fraud systems, they're unrelated to computing offline NDCG, and rollback capability doesn't depend on having one.

mcqs.question: Why do production recommendation systems set explicit per-stage latency budgets (e.g. 20-30ms for candidate generation, 40-60ms for ranking) instead of just one overall timeout?
options: Without a per-stage cap, a slower stage (like ranking) can silently consume time meant for another stage, risking the overall SLA with no visibility into which stage is actually the bottleneck
Because ANN search is not possible within any fixed time budget
Because ranking models are always faster than candidate generation, so budgets aren't really needed
Because regulations mandate a fixed latency budget per pipeline stage
mcqs.explanation: Per-stage budgets exist so no single stage can quietly eat another's time allowance, making bottlenecks visible and enforceable rather than only discovering an SLA breach after the fact. ANN search does run within tight budgets in practice, ranking is typically the slower stage (not faster), and there's no such regulatory mandate.

mcqs.question: Why are diversity caps and business rules (e.g. 'no more than 3 items per brand in the top 10') typically applied as a re-ranking pass rather than trained directly into the ranking model?
options: Ranking models are mathematically incapable of ever learning such a constraint
Business rules are not allowed to influence machine-learned rankings under any circumstances
Re-ranking passes always improve the model's offline relevance metric
It's easier to reason about, tune, and audit an explicit rule than to teach a scoring model an implicit property, and business rules can be adjusted instantly without retraining
mcqs.explanation: The deterministic post-processing layer is chosen for operational reasons — auditability and the ability to adjust a rule instantly — not because it's the only technically possible approach. A model could in principle learn soft versions of such constraints, but that's harder to control precisely; a re-ranking pass doesn't necessarily improve relevance metrics (that's not its goal), and business rules routinely do shape final rankings.

mcqs.question: Why can a recommendation system's own interaction logs be a biased training signal, even though they come from real user behavior?
options: Because interaction logs are always corrupted by bots

Users can only interact with what the system already chose to show, so items rarely surfaced accumulate little data regardless of true preference, creating a feedback loop that reinforces past exposure patterns
Because interaction logs cannot be stored for more than a few days
Because users never click on recommended items at all
mcqs.explanation: The bias comes from exposure, not corruption or storage limits: logs only reflect reactions to what was already surfaced, so under-shown items stay data-starved regardless of how much users might actually want them, and retraining on that data can compound the narrowing. Bot corruption and storage duration aren't the mechanism here, and users obviously do click on recommended items — that's exactly what generates the biased signal.
